title: Ontario attorney general urges Ottawa to strengthen self-defence rules in case of home invasions
summary: Ontario's attorney general and solicitor general have penned a letter to the federal government calling for clarified rules and stronger protections for home owners who protect themselves against…

image.caption: Ontario Attorney General Doug Downey, along with Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, called for increased protections for homeowners who protect themselves against home invasion in a letter to the federal government on Friday. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Ontario's attorney general and solicitor general have penned a letter to the federal government calling for clarified rules and stronger protections for home owners who protect themselves against home invasions. The letter comes amid an multiple violent home invasions in Toronto this fall, including one this week that left a man dead.
Letter to federal justice, public safety ministers calls for clarified rules, quicker assessments
The Ontario government is urging Ottawa to strengthen and clarify legal protections for homeowners who defend themselves against home invaders.

In a letter addressed to the federal ministers of justice and public safety Friday, Ontario Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner called for changes to Canada’s Criminal Code "to ensure that Canadians feel safe in their own homes and feel confident that they have the right to protect themselves and their families."

The letter proposes changes that would affirm a homeowner does not have to leave their home before relying on self-defence, explicitly recognize the circumstances of a home invasion in assessing the reasonableness of self-defence, and speed up assessments of whether or not defending oneself with force was warranted.

The call comes after the killing of 39-year-old Michael Eckert early on Wednesday, whom police say was shot by a suspect who had forced entry into his home. That incident happened weeks after another violent home invasion in the city's Bridle Path neighbourhood.

items: Here's where home invasions are happening in Toronto and what's being done to prevent them

blocks.text: At a news conference on Thursday, Premier Doug Ford said he supported legal changes to address the recent home invasions and would direct Downey and Kerzner to look into them.
"We will go right up as far as we can on the castle law," he said, referencing the laws that some U.S. states have that allow residents to use reasonable force to protect themselves in their homes.

Ford also urged people to defend themselves with force when confronted by a home invasion: "I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back," he said. "Use anything you can to protect your family."
Toronto police said in a news conference Wednesday that anyone facing a home invasion should call 911 first.
Doug Ford says he'd shoot home invaders: 'right through the front door'

Self-defence is already legal under the Criminal Code, which Friday's letter acknowledges. Under Sec. 34, a person can use force to defend themselves or another person against an act or threat of violence, as long as the force is "reasonable in the circumstances," which is determined by the court on a case-by-case basis.

In Toronto, home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.
